title: What counts as height work and how falls happen
audience: Trade and exterior service workers, leading hands and supervisors who plan or do any task above ground level, including on ladders, platforms, roofs and decks.
learningOutcomes: Describe which tasks count as height work on a service job, including the access route as well as the working position.
Name the main routes a worker can fall by on exterior and trade jobs.
Explain why a trigger height taken from another jurisdiction must be checked before use in Australia.
Identify the falling-object risks that apply below any elevated task and the control for each.

instruction.heading: Why the height is not the whole story
instruction.body: Many serious falls on trade and exterior jobs happen at heights the worker did not think of as work at height. Someone reaching a gutter from a bench, leaning over a balcony rail to wash a window, or standing on the highest step of a stepladder to change a light fitting is doing height work, even though nothing about the job feels dangerous. The useful question is not how high the job is in general, but what would happen if the worker lost their footing from their working position, or from the route they took to get there. One source ranks falls near the top of the causes of construction deaths; that comparison relates to an overseas industry and is not used in this lesson.

instruction.heading: Where the trigger sits
instruction.body: The sources in this pack do not agree on a trigger height. One training deck uses one fixed height figure as its trigger for height work. A contractor procedure applies fall protection from a fixed height, stated in imperial units. A third source takes a wider view and counts any position from which someone could be hurt by falling, including positions below ground level, and it treats the route up and down as part of the task. None of these figures is an Australian legal trigger. In New South Wales, a separate rule requires a construction safe work method statement where someone could fall more than two metres; that rule is confirmed in the project licence matrix, but it is not a general trigger for every service job. A business should therefore set its working rule from its own risk assessment and a checked state rule, and leave out any figure it has not checked.

instruction.heading: The routes a fall takes
instruction.body: The sources describe five main routes. The first is falling from an edge, such as a roof, balcony, deck, platform or the open side of a structure. The second is falling through an opening, or through a surface that cannot bear weight, such as a skylight, a rotten board, a translucent roof sheet or an uncovered floor hole. The third is falling from ladders and step equipment, through overreaching, slipping, a moving base or a tipping ladder. The fourth is falling from a platform that tips, runs away or lacks guard components. The fifth is falling into an excavation or pit, or from a lower level where a worker is leaning or working off balance. Each route needs a different control, so the risk assessment in “Writing a risk assessment for height work” names the route for every position.

instruction.heading: Falling objects belong to the same plan
instruction.body: A tool, a bucket, a length of flashing or a piece of glass that drops from height can seriously injure a person below. The controls are practical. Keep tools in pouches or on lanyards, keep materials well clear of the edge, cone or barricade the area beneath the work, and tell anyone below before anything is raised or lowered. Hand lines and purpose-built containers are safer than throwing items up or down.

instruction.heading: The route is part of the task
instruction.body: Getting up and getting down form part of the exposure. Two of the sources mention climbing with tools. A worker should keep both hands free while climbing, and should carry tools only in a belt built for that purpose. Heavier items should be hauled up or lowered inside a proper container. The route should be walked before the first climb, checked again after any change, and kept clear of trip hazards such as cables, hoses and debris.

instruction.heading: Weather and surface change the picture
instruction.body: Rain, ice, wind, heat and glare each change how well a person keeps their footing and how well they can see the surface. A wet roof tile or an icy deck board can turn a safe position into an unsafe one within minutes. Stop and reassess when conditions change, not only at the start of the day, and treat any weather limit the business has set as a stop condition.

procedure: Identify every position where the worker will stand, sit, kneel or lean above ground level or close to an edge.
Record the height of each position above the lower level, and the route used to reach it.
Name the fall type for each position: edge, opening, fragile surface, ladder or platform, or excavation.
Set the working trigger rule from the business plan and a checked state rule, and leave out any unchecked figure.
List the falling-object risks below and the area each control must cover.
Check the weather and the surface at the start of the task and again after any change.

workedExamples.situation: A technician cleans the gutters of a single-storey house from a ladder, then moves to a low balcony to reach the upper windows.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which positions count as work at height here, and what else must be checked?
workedExamples.reasoning: The ladder positions and the balcony are both elevated positions with a fall exposure. The ladder route and the balcony edge are both part of the task. The area below needs control because of falling debris and water.

workedExamples.situation: A handyman replaces deck boards above a drop to paving, and a tool bag sits on the deck edge.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: Which fall and falling-object hazards apply, and what is the first control to set?
workedExamples.reasoning: The deck edge is an open side and the drop counts as a fall hazard. The tool bag on the edge is a falling-object hazard. The first control is to move the tool bag back and to decide on an edge control before boards are removed near the edge.

workedExamples.situation: A worker must step onto an older tiled roof to check flashing, and some tiles look cracked.
workedExamples.decisionPrompt: What must happen before the worker steps onto the roof?
workedExamples.reasoning: A cracked or aged roof surface may not carry a person. Treat the surface as fragile, identify the controls in “Roof and fragile-surface work”, and do not step onto the tiles until those controls have been set up.

equipmentAndPpe: Ladder or access equipment checked before use (see “Choosing and using ladders for trade and exterior work”)
Tool pouches, belts and lanyards for hand tools
Hard hat with chin strap where falling objects are possible, as the business PPE rule requires
Non-slip footwear suited to the surface
Barrier tape or cones for the area below

commonErrors.error: Treating a task as low risk because the working height is only slightly above the floor.
commonErrors.prevention: Ask what a fall from that position would do, including from a stool or the top of a ladder, and apply the business trigger rule.

commonErrors.error: Assessing only the working position and ignoring the route up and down.
commonErrors.prevention: Include the route in the hazard entry and check it on arrival.

commonErrors.error: Assuming a trigger height from a foreign training deck applies in Australia.
commonErrors.prevention: Use the business rule and the checked state rule, and leave out any unchecked figure.

commonErrors.error: Dropping tools or materials from a ledge to the ground.
commonErrors.prevention: Lower items by container or hand line, and barricade the area below before anything moves.

safetyAndRegulatory.point: Warning: falls from height cause some of the most serious injuries in trade work. Where a position may allow a fall, do not start until the fall control in the job plan is in place.
Trigger heights differ between jurisdictions and between sources. Confirm the state or territory rule before relying on any trigger figure.

Licence notice: this lesson does not grant a licence, certificate or authority to work at height. Some elevated work sits under high risk work licensing in some states (see “Scaffold and mobile tower checks before use” and “Elevated work platform pre-use checks”). The lesson does not state where that applies.
Stop-work rule: if a position may allow a fall and no control is in place, stop and tell the supervisor before any further climbing or stepping onto the surface.

qualityStandard: Every elevated position and its route is listed in the job plan.
Each position has a named fall type.
The trigger rule used is written, and any unchecked state figure is left out.
Falling-object controls for the area below are recorded.
documentationEvidence: Job plan or hazard entry listing positions, heights, routes and fall types
Note of the trigger rule applied and where it came from
summary: Work at height includes the position, the route to it and the surface you stand on.
Trigger heights differ between sources and states; a foreign figure is not an Australian rule.
Falling objects below an elevated task are part of the same plan.
Weather and surface conditions can turn a safe position into a stop condition.

knowledgeChecks.question: A worker reaches a gutter by standing on the highest step of a step ladder. Which statement is correct?
options: The position is not work at height because the ladder is a short step ladder.
The top step and the route up the ladder are part of the height task and must be assessed.
Only the ladder rating needs checking, because the position is low.
Work at height starts only above the second storey of a building.

knowledgeChecks.question: Which of these is a fall route that must be considered on a job?
options: Falling through a skylight or a worn board on a roof surface
Carrying a bag of tools up a driveway and then a short walk
Pressure washing a paved path at ground level in the rain
Walking across a level kitchen floor with a mop in hand

knowledgeChecks.question: Why must an Australian business check a trigger height taken from a foreign training deck before using it?
options: Foreign training decks give heights in imperial units only and the decks are rarely updated
Trigger rules and figures differ by jurisdiction, so the figure in the deck may not match the Australian rule.
Australian law has no trigger height for any work and the decks have no ladder rules at all
The figure in the deck is too high to matter for a short ladder and the ladder is always fixed in place
